explanations.explanation: That's the ask, baker. He kneels and says, “Lord, if You are willing, You can make me clean.” I think there's a lot packed into that little “…if You are willing…” He says what he believes Jesus can do and leaves the rest in Jesus' hands.

The text never mentions his family, friend. He kneels and says, “Lord, if You are willing, You can make me clean.” Being made clean is the one thing he asks for. He doesn't ask for anything else on the side.

Money never comes up here, baker. I'd get down on my knees for a wiped-clean credit card bill too, but that's not this man's request. He says, “Lord, if You are willing, You can make me clean.” His whole request is that one line.

explanations.answer: He reaches out and touches him
explanations.explanation: Jesus reached out His hand and touched the man. Then He said, “I am willing… Be clean!” (Matthew 8:3) The touch comes right there with the words. Friend, I can tell you I would have stood there a second just taking that in.

explanations.answer: He tells him to wash in the Jordan
explanations.explanation: No river trip in this one, baker. Jesus doesn't send him anywhere to wash. The text says He reached out His hand and touched the man, and then He spoke.

explanations.answer: He puts mud on his skin
explanations.explanation: No mud in this scene, friend. Jesus reaches out His hand and touches the man, then says, “I am willing… Be clean!” (Matthew 8:3) A hand and a word are all the text gives us here. My kitchen gets messier than this.

The text says it didn't take days, baker. After Jesus says “Be clean!” the verse says, “And immediately his leprosy was cleansed.” There's no waiting period. Even my cookies need a good twelve minutes in the oven, and this took no time at all.
That's right, baker. The text says, “And immediately his leprosy was cleansed.” There's no few days of waiting. Jesus says the word and the healing is done.

Jesus says, “But go, show yourself to the priest and offer the gift prescribed by Moses, as a testimony to them.” After the healing, the priest is the one He sends the man to. I'd love to have seen that priest's face, friend.
Elders aren't mentioned here, friend. Jesus tells the man, “…go, show yourself to the priest…” That's who he's sent to. The gift he offers is the one prescribed by Moses.

Close, but the text says something else, baker. Jesus doesn't send him to a prophet. He says, “…go, show yourself to the priest and offer the gift prescribed by Moses…” The priest is the one he's sent to see.

That's him, baker. The centurion says, “Lord, my servant lies at home, paralyzed and in terrible agony.” He's an army officer, and he's come to plead for someone else. I think that tells you something about how he sees his servant.

The text doesn't mention a son, friend. The centurion says, “Lord, my servant lies at home, paralyzed and in terrible agony.” He's pleading for his servant, someone in his household. Nobody else in his family is named.
No brother in this story, baker. The centurion says, “Lord, my servant lies at home, paralyzed and in terrible agony.” The one he's pleading for is his servant. That's the whole request.
Yes, friend. Jesus replies, “I will go and heal him…” Those are His words after the centurion tells Him about his servant. He says He'll go and heal him.
The text says the opposite, baker. Jesus replies, “I will go and heal him…” He says He'll come. If you picked False, you only missed a detail.

explanations.answer: Having Jesus come under his roof
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The centurion says, “Lord, I am not worthy to have You come under my roof.” He keeps calling Jesus Lord, too.
Speaking up isn't the issue, friend. The centurion has already come and pleaded with Jesus. What he says he isn't worthy of is having Jesus come under his roof (Matthew 8:8).

He actually keeps asking, baker. He pleads with Jesus for his servant, and he even tells Him, “But just say the word, and my servant will be healed.” The thing he says he isn't worthy of is having Jesus come under his roof (Matthew 8:8). The asking is not the problem.
Yes, baker. He says, “But just say the word, and my servant will be healed.” He isn't asking Jesus to come under his roof. Just a word.
He's not asking for a day, friend. The centurion isn't scheduling anything. He says, “But just say the word, and my servant will be healed.” The word is what he asks for.
Nobody talks money here, baker. The centurion doesn't name a price or offer a payment. He says, “But just say the word, and my servant will be healed.” All he asks for is the word.

explanations.answer: He knows a command gets obeyed
explanations.explanation: That's his point, baker. He says, “For I myself am a man under authority, with soldiers under me. I tell one to go, and he goes, and another to come, and he comes.” Then he adds that his servant does what he's told. I think he's saying a word from Jesus is all it takes, because that's what he's just asked for.

explanations.answer: He wants Jesus to see his rank
explanations.explanation: Rank isn't what he's showing off, friend. The centurion says he is “…a man under authority…” He has soldiers under him, but he's under someone too. And he started by saying he isn't worthy, so I don't think he's bragging.

explanations.answer: He offers his men to guard Jesus
explanations.explanation: No guard duty in this story, baker. The centurion never offers his soldiers to Jesus. He talks about how his orders get obeyed: “I tell one to go, and he goes, and another to come, and he comes.”

explanations.answer: He hasn't found faith this great in Israel
explanations.explanation: That's what He says, baker. Jesus says, “Truly I tell you, I have not found anyone in Israel with such great faith.” Think about that. The man who gets this praise is an army officer who asked for a word.

explanations.answer: It's as small as a mustard seed for now
explanations.explanation: Jesus says the opposite, friend. He calls it “…such great faith.” There's nothing small about it. The text says He marveled at the centurion, and then He said, “…I have not found anyone in Israel with such great faith.”

explanations.answer: It will grow if he keeps on asking
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that, baker. Jesus doesn't talk about the faith growing later. He says, “…I have not found anyone in Israel with such great faith.” It's already great.

Yes, baker. Jesus says many “…will come from the east and the west to share the banquet with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven.” So the guests come from far and wide, and what they share is the banquet. A banquet is right up my alley, friend, and mine would have cookies on every plate.
Not quite, friend. Jesus doesn't say inheritance here. He says many will come “…to share the banquet with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven.” The banquet is what's on the table.
Covenant isn't the word Jesus uses, baker. He says many will come “…to share the banquet with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven.” What they share is the banquet.
That's it, baker. Jesus tells the centurion, “Go! As you have believed, so will it be done for you.” It's tied to his believing. His servant is healed at that very hour.

Earning isn't the word, friend. Jesus says, “As you have believed, so will it be done for you.” He ties it to believing, not earning. The centurion himself says, “…I am not worthy to have You come under my roof.”

Serving isn't what Jesus says here, baker. He tells the centurion, “Go! As you have believed, so will it be done for you.” The word is believed. Serving shows up later in this passage, when Peter's mother-in-law gets up (Matthew 8:15).

Yes, baker. The text says, “And his servant was healed at that very hour.” Jesus has just told the centurion, “Go! As you have believed, so will it be done for you.” The healing is recorded right after those words.

The text says the opposite, friend. “And his servant was healed at that very hour.” That's what the text records, right after Jesus says, “Go! As you have believed, so will it be done for you.” So this one is True.

explanations.answer: She gets up and serves Him
explanations.explanation: That's what she does, baker. The text says, “…the fever left her, and she got up and began to serve Him.” The fever leaves, and she's up on her feet. Imagine going from a sickbed to serving, friend. I can't even get off the couch after a long day of stamping.
Not this time, friend. The text says the fever left her, “…and she got up and began to serve Him.” Getting up and serving is what it says she does. Sleeping isn't mentioned.

explanations.answer: She runs to tell the neighbors
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that, baker. It says, “…the fever left her, and she got up and began to serve Him.” She's on her feet and serving. Nothing is said about neighbors.
The text says something bigger, baker. It says Jesus “…drove out the spirits with a word and healed all the sick.” That's all of them. There's nobody left out of that evening line.
Yes, friend. The text says Jesus “…drove out the spirits with a word and healed all the sick.” Every sick person brought to Him that evening was healed. There's no left-behind group in that line.

That's him, baker. The text says this “…was to fulfill what was spoken through the prophet Isaiah…” Then it quotes, “He took up our infirmities and carried our diseases.” The words are credited to the prophet Isaiah.

Moses is in this passage, friend, but he's not the one quoted here. Jesus mentions the gift prescribed by Moses back in verse 4. The words about infirmities and diseases come “…through the prophet Isaiah…”

Not David this time, baker. Matthew says this was to fulfill what was spoken “…through the prophet Isaiah…” The quote is “He took up our infirmities and carried our diseases.” So the speaker here is Isaiah, a prophet.
